sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: File I/O questions test whether you understand Go's composition-based standard library. The `io.Reader` and `io.Writer` interfaces are arguably Go's most important interfaces — everything from files to HTTP response bodies to in-memory buffers satisfies them. For freshers, understanding why Go code uses interfaces instead of concrete types is what makes this module valuable beyond just knowing how to read a file.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
One interface pattern that ties everything together:

- **`io.Reader` and `io.Writer` are the universal connectors.** `os.File`, `http.Response.Body`, `bytes.Buffer`, `strings.Reader`, `gzip.Reader` — all satisfy `io.Reader`. A function that accepts `io.Reader` works with any of them without modification. This is Go's alternative to Java's verbose InputStream/OutputStream hierarchy.
- **`defer f.Close()` immediately after `os.Open`** — not at the end of the function, not after error checking, but right after open succeeds. This way you never forget to close the file even if the function has multiple return paths.
- **`bufio` wraps a Reader/Writer with a buffer** — reduces the number of syscalls for large file operations from one per byte/line to one per buffer-full. For reading a file line by line, `bufio.Scanner` is the idiomatic tool.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **os.Open, os.Create, os.ReadFile** — `os.ReadFile(path)` reads entire file to `[]byte` (simple but not for large files); `os.Open(path)` returns `*os.File` for streaming reads; `os.Create(path)` creates or truncates for writes
- **defer close pattern** — `f, err := os.Open(path); if err != nil { return err }; defer f.Close()` — defer goes right after the nil check
- **bufio.Scanner and bufio.Writer** — `scanner := bufio.NewScanner(f); for scanner.Scan() { line := scanner.Text() }` for line-by-line reading; `w := bufio.NewWriter(f); w.WriteString(...); w.Flush()` for buffered writes
- **io.Reader and io.Writer interfaces** — `Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)` and `Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)`; composable with `io.TeeReader`, `io.MultiReader`, `io.LimitReader`
- **io.Copy** — `io.Copy(dst io.Writer, src io.Reader)` efficiently copies from src to dst without loading everything into memory; used for file copies, proxying HTTP responses
- **filepath package** — `filepath.Join("dir", "file.txt")` for platform-independent paths (avoids hardcoded `/` vs `\`); `filepath.Ext`, `filepath.Base`, `filepath.Dir`
- **Environment variables** — `os.Getenv("PORT")` returns empty string if not set; `os.LookupEnv("PORT")` returns value and ok bool to distinguish unset from empty

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Forgetting to close a file** — not calling `f.Close()` leaks a file descriptor. The OS has a limit (typically 1024 per process). Under load, a service that leaks file descriptors will eventually fail with 'too many open files'.
- **`scanner.Scan()` has a default 64 KB line limit** — very long lines cause `scanner.Err()` to return an error. In an interview, mention that for arbitrary input you should check `scanner.Err()` after the loop, and for long lines use `bufio.Reader.ReadString`.
- **`io.Copy` does not load the entire file into memory** — it copies in chunks. Interviewers ask: 'how would you copy a 10 GB file?' — the answer is `io.Copy`, not `os.ReadFile`.
- **`filepath.Join` vs string concatenation** — `"dir" + "/" + "file"` breaks on Windows. Always use `filepath.Join`. This is a standard code review comment.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"For simple file reads I use `os.ReadFile` which loads the whole file into a `[]byte`. For large files I use `os.Open` followed immediately by `defer f.Close()`, then wrap it in `bufio.Scanner` for line-by-line reading. The reason I reach for `bufio` is that it reduces the number of syscalls by buffering reads in memory. The key insight about Go's I/O design is that `io.Reader` and `io.Writer` are universal interfaces — the same code that reads from a file can read from an HTTP response body or an in-memory buffer without any changes."*
